lead: This unit explains how the body makes tiny voltages, how electrodes pick them up, and how recorders turn them into ECG, EEG and EMG traces. After it you can read a bio-potential block diagram, choose an electrode, set amplifier gain and CMRR, and explain Holter, NCV, evoked potential and gait measurements.
about: The unit starts with the cell membrane: 1.1 derives resting and action potentials. 1.2 turns that voltage source into an electrode–electrolyte circuit and compares surface, needle and microelectrodes. 1.3 covers transducers, especially the strain-gauge load cell. 1.4 builds the bio-amplifier and data-acquisition chain. 1.5 to 1.8 apply the chain to ECG, vectorcardiography, EEG, EMG, nerve conduction velocity, heart-rate and Holter monitoring, with maintenance and troubleshooting. 1.9 extends EEG to multichannel montages, epilepsy, evoked potentials and MEG. 1.10 closes the loop with EEG and EMG biofeedback. 1.11 measures the mechanical body: foot pressure, gait and limb position. Each chapter uses the previous one, so the recorder is built piece by piece.

chapters.idea: A living cell maintains a negative resting voltage and fires a brief positive action potential when threshold is crossed.
chapters.depth: Cover the cell membrane, ion pumps, concentration gradients, Nernst and Goldman ideas in words, resting potential usually near -70 mV inside, threshold, depolarisation, repolarisation, hyperpolarisation, refractory period, and the all-or-none action potential. Some syllabi call this electrophysiology or bioelectric potentials. Keep numerical Nernst calculation short; name sodium-potassium pump and leak channels. Show a typical waveform and define mV, ms and threshold. One line: this is the source every recorder measures.

figure.aria: A plot of membrane voltage in millivolts against time in milliseconds, showing rest at -70 mV, threshold at -55 mV, peak at +30 mV, and return to rest.

chapters.example: A neuron has resting potential -70 mV, threshold -55 mV and peak +30 mV. Find the depolarisation needed to reach threshold and the peak-to-peak amplitude. Answer: 15 mV and 100 mV.
chapters.trap: Resting potential is negative inside the cell; threshold is a depolarised value, not the resting value.
chapters.prereq: School-level idea of a cell membrane and ions.
chapters.leave: Detailed ion-channel kinetics and clinical nerve physiology to physiology courses; Unit 2 uses the ECG, not the cell model.

chapters.idea: An electrode converts ionic current in tissue into electronic current in wires through a double layer, and its impedance must match the amplifier.
chapters.depth: Cover the electrode–electrolyte interface, half-cell potential, polarisation, offset voltage, electrode impedance, Ag/AgCl and reusable versus disposable electrodes. Compare surface electrodes (plate, suction, floating), needle electrodes (concentric, monopolar) and microelectrodes (glass micropipette, metal microelectrode, tip resistance). Some syllabi call this electrode theory; include bipolar and unipolar arrangements. Keep the Nernst equation only as a name; focus on the equivalent circuit and safety.

figure.title: Electrode–electrolyte path
figure.aria: A block diagram of the electrode path from metal electrode through double layer, electrolyte gel and skin tissue to a reference electrode.

chapters.example: A glass microelectrode has tip resistance 10 MΩ. The amplifier input impedance is 1 GΩ. What fraction of the bio-potential reaches the amplifier, and what is the loss? Answer: 1 GΩ/(1 GΩ + 10 MΩ) = 0.9901; about 99% reaches the amplifier and about 1% is lost.
chapters.trap: Do not add electrode offset to the signal as if it were real bio-potential; it is a DC half-cell potential and must be blocked or balanced.
chapters.leave: Biosensor recognition layers and ISFETs to Unit 4; electrode sterilisation practice to hospital training.

chapters.idea: A physiological transducer changes a body variable such as force, pressure or temperature into an electrical signal, and the load cell does this with strain gauges in a bridge.
chapters.depth: Cover selection criteria: range, sensitivity, linearity, hysteresis, accuracy, resolution, loading effect and biocompatibility. Cover resistive, capacitive, inductive, piezoelectric and photoelectric transducers in brief. Explain strain gauge, gauge factor, quarter/half/full bridge, load cell construction and applications in weighing and biomechanics. Some syllabi call this physiological transducers and selection criteria. Include temperature sensors as a short comparison, not full details.

figure.title: Load cell chain
figure.aria: A block diagram from body force to strain gauge, Wheatstone bridge, amplifier, ADC and display.

chapters.example: A quarter-bridge load cell uses 350 Ω strain gauges, excitation 5 V and gauge factor 2.0. The strain is 1000 µε (1×10⁻³). Find the bridge output. Answer: ΔV = V_ex × GF × ε/4 = 5 × 2 × 0.001/4 = 0.0025 V = 2.5 mV.
chapters.trap: In a quarter bridge only one gauge is active, so the output is one quarter of the full-bridge value for the same strain.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2; basic circuit laws and the Wheatstone bridge.
chapters.leave: Pressure transducers for blood pressure and respiration to Unit 2; biosensor transducers to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A bio-amplifier must take a small differential signal riding on a large common-mode voltage and pass it cleanly to an ADC.
chapters.depth: Cover differential and instrumentation amplifiers, gain, input impedance, CMRR, input offset, noise, bandwidth, isolation, driven right leg, filters (high-pass for offset, low-pass for noise, notch for 50 Hz), and data acquisition: sample-and-hold, multiplexer, ADC resolution, sampling rate and Nyquist. Some syllabi call this bio-amplifiers and DAS. Include block level only; op-amp internal design is not needed.

figure.title: Bio-amplifier and DAS
figure.aria: A block diagram from electrodes through protection, instrumentation amplifier, filters, ADC, MCU and display.

chapters.example: A bio-amplifier has gain 1000 and CMRR 80 dB. The differential input is 1 mV and the common-mode input is 50 mV. Find the output signal and the output interference. Answer: CMRR ratio = 10⁴; common-mode gain = 1000/10⁴ = 0.1; signal output = 1 V; interference output = 0.1 × 50 mV = 5 mV.
chapters.trap: CMRR in dB must be converted to a ratio before calculating common-mode output; 80 dB is 10⁴, not 80.
chapters.leave: Op-amp internal circuits to electronics; DAS hardware and software in biosensors to Unit 4; electrical safety to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The ECG recorder amplifies the heart's millivolt signal through standard leads and displays P, QRS and T waves on a calibrated time and voltage grid.
chapters.depth: Cover standard 12 leads, Einthoven triangle, unipolar and bipolar leads, ECG block diagram, calibration 1 mV = 10 mm, paper speed 25 mm/s, normal wave durations and amplitudes (P, PR, QRS, ST, T), common abnormal waves, and vectorcardiography with Frank leads and the QRS loop. Some syllabi call vectorcardiography VCG. Keep arrhythmia diagnosis to Unit 2; here focus on the recording chain.

figure.title: ECG recording chain
figure.aria: A block diagram from ECG electrodes to lead selector, buffer, bio-amplifier, filters, ADC and ECG display, with a branch to a Frank lead network and VCG loop.

chapters.example: An ECG is recorded at 25 mm/s with calibration 1 mV = 10 mm. The RR interval is 18 mm and the QRS width is 2.0 mm. Find the heart rate and QRS duration. Answer: RR = 18/25 = 0.72 s; heart rate = 60/0.72 = 83.3 bpm; QRS = 2/25 = 0.08 s = 80 ms.
chapters.trap: Paper speed sets time and calibration sets voltage; a normal-looking shape is still wrong if the 1 mV calibration bar is not 10 mm.
chapters.leave: Arrhythmia and foetal ECG monitoring to Unit 2; defibrillator protection to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: EEG records cortical postsynaptic potentials in microvolts, while EMG records muscle fibre action potentials in millivolts, so each needs its own band, gain and filter.
chapters.depth: Cover EEG electrode placement in the 10–20 system, referential and bipolar montages, alpha/beta/theta/delta bands, gain around 10⁴, bandwidth 0.5–70 Hz and artefacts. Cover EMG surface and needle electrodes, motor unit action potential, bandwidth 20–500 Hz, gain, rectification, RMS, and fatigue as a shift in frequency and amplitude. Some syllabi call this EEG and EMG recording; include analysis and fatigue characteristics at block level. Do not cover epilepsy or evoked potentials in detail here.

figure.title: EEG and EMG branches
figure.aria: A block diagram with shared electrodes splitting into EEG amplifier, EEG filter and EEG display, and into EMG amplifier, EMG filter and EMG display.

chapters.example: An EEG amplifier has gain 10,000 and input 50 µV. What is the output? If the EEG is sampled at 250 Hz, what is the Nyquist frequency? Answer: output = 50 µV × 10,000 = 0.5 V; Nyquist = 250/2 = 125 Hz.
chapters.trap: EEG is in microvolts and EMG in millivolts; using the same gain and filter for both will clip EMG or bury EEG in noise.
chapters.leave: Epilepsy, multichannel montages, evoked potentials and MEG to Chapter 9; biofeedback to Chapter 10.

chapters.idea: Nerve conduction velocity equals the distance between two stimulation sites divided by the difference in response latency.
chapters.depth: Cover motor and sensory NCV, surface stimulation, recording electrodes, CMAP and SNAP, latency, amplitude, distance measurement, temperature effect, and the formula v = d/Δt. Some syllabi call this nerve conduction studies. Keep needle EMG analysis to Chapter 6 and nerve stimulators to Unit 5. Mention that latency difference removes distal delay.

figure.aria: A timeline showing a stimulus at 0 ms, a distal response at 2 ms and a proximal response at 6 ms, so the latency difference is 4 ms.

chapters.example: The distance between distal and proximal stimulation sites is 200 mm. The distal latency is 2 ms and the proximal latency is 6 ms. Find the nerve conduction velocity. Answer: Δt = 4 ms; v = 200 mm/4 ms = 50 m/s.
chapters.trap: Use the latency difference, not one absolute latency, or distal nerve and muscle delay will make the velocity too low.
chapters.leave: Muscle and nerve stimulators to Unit 5 electrotherapy; clinical interpretation of neuropathy to medicine.

chapters.idea: A heart-rate monitor counts QRS events, a Holter records ECG for 24 hours, and troubleshooting separates patient, electrode, amplifier and interference faults.
chapters.depth: Cover QRS detection, RR interval, averaged heart rate, alarms, Holter cassette or flash memory, replay and scanning, ECG maintenance: calibration, electrode check, cable check, 50 Hz interference, baseline wander, muscle artefact and lead off. Some syllabi call this heart rate monitor and Holter monitor; include ECG machine maintenance and troubleshooting. Do not reteach ECG waves.

figure.title: Heart-rate and Holter path
figure.aria: A block diagram from ECG electrodes to QRS detector, RR timer and heart-rate display, with a branch from ECG electrodes to Holter recorder, memory and replay.

chapters.example: A 24-hour Holter record contains 108,000 QRS complexes. Find the average heart rate. Answer: 108,000/(24 × 60) = 75 bpm.
chapters.trap: Average heart rate is total beats divided by total minutes; do not divide by hours and call the answer bpm.
chapters.leave: Arrhythmia alarms and foetal monitoring to Unit 2; electrical safety testing to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Multichannel EEG maps brain activity across many electrodes, epilepsy and evoked potentials pull small signals out of background, and MEG measures the magnetic field of the same currents.
chapters.depth: Cover 10–20 and denser montages, referential versus bipolar, epileptic spikes and seizures in EEG, visual, auditory and somatosensory evoked potentials, averaging, latency and amplitude, and MEG with SQUID sensors. Some syllabi call these EPs VEP, BAEP and SSEP. MEG is advanced; only a few universities teach the SQUID details. Keep the averaging formula and artefact rejection; no clinical drug treatment.

figure.title: Multichannel EEG, EP and MEG
figure.aria: A block diagram of 10–20 electrodes through multichannel amplifier and montage to EEG display, a stimulus through averager to EP display, and MEG sensors through SQUID array to MEG display.

chapters.example: A visual evoked potential is 1 µV and the background EEG noise is 2 µV. Averaging improves SNR by √N. How many trials give an SNR of 10? Answer: single-trial SNR = 1/2 = 0.5; 0.5√N = 10; √N = 20; N = 400 trials.
chapters.trap: Averaging reduces random noise, not fixed artefacts; 50 Hz interference or eye blinks must be removed before averaging.
chapters.leave: Epilepsy treatment and EEG clinical reporting to medicine; MEG physics in depth is advanced.

chapters.idea: Biofeedback instrumentation turns a tiny EEG or EMG signal into a visible or audible signal so the patient can learn to change it.
chapters.depth: Cover the feedback loop: electrodes, high-gain amplifier, band-pass filter, rectifier, smoother, threshold comparator, tone or light display, and patient. Cover EEG alpha training and EMG relaxation training, thresholds, artefacts and safety. Some syllabi call this EEG biofeedback and EMG biofeedback; only a few universities teach full loop design. Keep EEG and EMG basics to Chapter 6.

figure.title: Biofeedback loop
figure.aria: A block diagram of a biofeedback loop from patient to electrodes, amplifier, filter, rectifier, threshold and tone or light, then back to the patient.

chapters.example: Raw EMG is 20 µV. The biofeedback amplifier gain is 1000. The comparator threshold is 15 mV. Is the tone on? Answer: output = 20 µV × 1000 = 20 mV; 20 mV > 15 mV, so yes, the tone is on.
chapters.trap: The feedback must follow the chosen band; an EMG biofeedback unit that also passes 50 Hz will reward interference, not muscle activity.
chapters.leave: Nerve and muscle stimulators to Unit 5; clinical training protocols to physiotherapy.

chapters.idea: Biomechanical measurement converts force, pressure and position into numbers for gait, foot loading and limb motion.
chapters.depth: Cover pedobarograph: pressure platform or insole, sensor arrays, calibration, peak pressure and contact area. Cover gait cycle: stance, swing, step length, stride length, cadence and speed. Cover limb position: goniometers, accelerometers, inertial sensors, camera markers, velocity and acceleration. Some syllabi call this biomechanics measurement; include load cell use from Chapter 3. Keep force-plate electronics short.

figure.aria: A gait timeline of one 1000 ms cycle, with stance from 0 to 600 ms and swing from 600 to 1000 ms.

chapters.example: A walker has step length 0.7 m and cadence 120 steps/min. Find speed. If stance is 60% of a 1.0 s gait cycle, find stance and swing times. Answer: cadence = 2 steps/s; speed = 0.7 × 2 = 1.4 m/s; stance = 0.6 s; swing = 0.4 s.
chapters.trap: Cadence is steps per minute, not strides per minute; one stride is two steps.
chapters.leave: Force-plate strain gauge design to Chapter 3; orthopaedic diagnosis to medicine.

links: resting and action potentials become the ionic source at the electrode
electrode impedance and signal level set transducer and amplifier needs
load cell bridge output needs a bio-amplifier and ADC
the amplifier chain becomes the ECG recorder
ECG recording leads to heart-rate and Holter monitoring
EEG and EMG recording extend to multichannel EEG and evoked potentials
EEG and EMG signals feed biofeedback loops
latency and gait timing both use time-distance measurement
